medium.titulo: What Happens When You Click a Button? Software Architecture, Series: 1
medium.resumo: When learning to code, most of us start with functions, components, or simple queries. But when it comes to building scalable, resilient…
medium.conteudo_html:
When learning to code, most of us start with functions, components, or simple queries. But when it comes to building scalable, resilient, and large-scale systems, code itself becomes just a small piece of the puzzle.

On my journey toward becoming a Software Architect, the rule I set for myself is simple: understand the big picture first, not just the code.

Phase 0 — the first step of this series — is about naming the components of a system and clearly picturing the answer to this fundamental question:

“How does a single request travel from the browser all the way to the database and back?”

The Big Picture: Where Does the Request Go?

When we view systems not as a single monolithic block, but as specialized layers communicating with one another, the flow broadly looks like this:

Now, let’s follow a request’s journey step by step. As an example, a user visits [https://shop.com/orders/42].

The Journey, Step by Step

  • DNS: The browser translates the domain shop.com into an IP address. DNS is essentially the phonebook of the internet.
  • Establishing the Connection: The browser and server first establish a TCP connection, followed by an encrypted TLS channel. In short, HTTPS = HTTP + TLS.
  • HTTP Request: The browser dispatches a payload containing the HTTP method (GET), the path (/orders/42), headers (Authorization: Bearer <token>), and a request body if needed.
  • Load Balancer: There might be 5 replicas of the same application running in the background. The load balancer routes the request to one of the healthy instances. Typically, TLS termination (decryption) happens here as well.
  • API Gateway: The single point of entry for the system. It verifies whether the token is valid (authentication) and checks if the rate limit has been exceeded (rate limiting). It routes requests starting with /orders to the Order Service, and those starting with /users to the User Service.
  • Service: This is where the core business logic executes. It verifies permissions — “Is this user authorized to view this order?” (authorization). Next, data is retrieved: it checks the cache first. If found (cache hit), it returns immediately; if not (cache miss), it queries the database.
  • Database: The service runs a query (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 42). The result is returned to the service and typically written back to the cache to speed up subsequent requests.
  • The Return Path: The response travels back along the same path: service → gateway → load balancer → browser. The browser receives a 200 OK status along with a JSON payload and renders the UI.

Key Concepts: A Quick Glossary

Communication Layer

  • Client: The initiator of the request (browser, mobile app).
  • Server: The receiver handling the request.
  • HTTP: The communication protocol governing how clients and servers exchange messages. It consists of requests and responses.
  • API: A system’s publicly exposed contract. Essentially: “Send a request to this endpoint in this format, and you will receive this response.”
  • REST: An architectural style for designing APIs. The URL represents a resource, and the HTTP method defines the action: GET /orders/42 (read), POST /orders (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (delete).

Traffic Layer

  • Load Balancer: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers. If an instance goes down, it reroutes traffic to healthy nodes.
  • API Gateway: Centralizes cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and routing in one place, preventing each service from having to reimplement them.
  • Service: A focused application responsible for a specific business domain (e.g., User Service, Order Service).

Data Layer

  • Database: Stores structured, persistent data (e.g., users, orders). Data remains safe even if the server shuts down.
  • Cache: Keeps frequently read data in memory / RAM (such as Redis). Extremely fast, but transient.
  • Storage: Dedicated object storage (such as AWS S3) for files like images, videos, and PDFs. These should not be stored directly inside relational databases.

Asynchronous Layer

  • Queue & Message Broker: Tasks such as sending an order confirmation email or decrementing inventory should not block the user. The Order Service drops an event or message into a message broker (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka) and immediately tells the user, “Your order has been received.” Another service pulls the message from the queue and handles the work in the background. This happens out-of-band, away from the synchronous request-response path.

Security

  • Authentication (AuthN): “Who are you?” Is the user logged in? Is the token valid? If not, return 401 Unauthorized.
  • Authorization (AuthZ): “Are you allowed to do this?” The identity is known, but do they have permission to access someone else’s order? If not, return 403 Forbidden.

15. What’s Next?

This was only the beginning.

In the next part, I want to go one level deeper into the backend itself.

I’ll explore concepts such as:

Controller
Service
DTO
Entity
Repository
Dependency Injection

And more importantly, I’ll try to understand:

What happens to a request after it reaches the backend?

My goal isn’t simply to learn another framework or become someone who can write backend code.

I want to understand how the different pieces of a software system fit together, how architectural decisions are made, and eventually how to design systems myself.

This is just Series #1.

medium.titulo: How to Create, Edit, and Publish Surveys Directly in Claude with SurveyFlip MCP
medium.resumo: Creating a survey shouldn’t require a dozen tabs, a blank form, and an hour of clicking.
medium.conteudo_html:
Creating a survey shouldn’t require a dozen tabs, a blank form, and an hour of clicking.

Yet that’s still how many teams build surveys today.

Open the survey platform. Choose a template. Add a question. Select a question type. Add answer choices. Edit the wording. Rearrange questions. Check the settings. Save the draft. Preview it. Go back and fix something. Publish it. Copy the link. Then send it to your audience.

None of these steps is particularly difficult.

The problem is that they add friction between having a research question and actually asking it.

Now imagine describing the survey you want in plain English and having an AI assistant help create it inside your survey platform.

That’s the idea behind AI survey creation MCP.

With the SurveyFlip MCP Server connected to Claude, you can use natural-language instructions to create a SurveyFlip draft, add questions, modify questions, set survey dates, publish the survey, and retrieve its public link.

You don’t have to treat survey creation as a series of disconnected clicks.

You can treat it as a conversation.

For example:

“Create a six-question customer satisfaction survey for a B2B SaaS product. Keep it short, include a 1–10 opinion scale, ask about the biggest problem customers face, and save it as a draft.”

Claude can translate that request into survey-building actions through the SurveyFlip connection.

You can then review the draft and continue:

“Change question three to a multiple-choice question and add an option for ‘Other.’”

Then:

“Set the survey to end seven days after it starts.”

And when you’re ready:

“Publish the survey.”

This is more than a shortcut for creating questions.

It represents a different way to interact with survey software.

In this guide, we’ll explain how SurveyFlip MCP Server enables AI-assisted survey creation, how to create and edit surveys with Claude, how publishing works, which question types are supported, practical prompts for different research teams, and how to build a reliable conversational survey workflow.

What Is AI Survey Creation With Claude and SurveyFlip?

AI survey creation with Claude uses natural-language instructions to help build surveys through a connected survey platform. With the SurveyFlip MCP Server, Claude can create a draft, add and modify supported questions, configure dates, publish the survey, and provide its public link after the appropriate confirmation.

The important distinction is between generating survey copy and actually creating a survey.

An AI assistant can already write survey questions in a chat window.

But that still leaves you with another job:

Copy the questions → Open SurveyFlip → Create the survey → Add each question → Configure choices → Publish

An MCP-connected workflow can reduce that gap.

The process becomes:

Describe → Create draft → Review → Edit → Publish → Share

That means the AI isn’t simply helping you brainstorm a questionnaire.

It can help operate the survey workflow itself.

This is where the Model Context Protocol becomes useful.

MCP provides a standardized way for AI applications to interact with external tools. In this case, the SurveyFlip MCP Server gives Claude access to supported SurveyFlip capabilities.

The result is a conversational interface for survey management.

Why Traditional Survey Creation Has Too Much Friction

A survey might look simple to the respondent.

For the person building it, there’s usually much more involved.

Consider a product manager who wants to understand why users aren’t adopting a new feature.

The research plan might be straightforward:

  1. Ask whether customers have used the feature.
  2. Ask how useful they find it.
  3. Ask what prevents adoption.
  4. Ask what would make it more useful.
  5. Ask for additional feedback.

That’s a five-question survey.

But building it manually still requires several decisions.

Which question type should you use?

Instead of exporting a CSV and manually sorting through hundreds of responses, you can ask Claude to analyze the available survey data, identify themes, summarize feedback, and help surface the questions that deserve deeper investigation.

That’s where survey creation starts connecting with survey analysis.

And that’s the larger opportunity:

Not just AI-generated surveys.

Not just AI-generated summaries.

An AI-assisted survey lifecycle from the first research question to the final decision.

If you haven’t connected SurveyFlip to Claude yet, start with our setup guide:

How to Connect SurveyFlip MCP Server to Claude

Then create your first draft with a simple instruction:

“Create a six-question survey to help me understand [your research problem]. Save it as a draft.”

Review it.

Ask questions.

Make changes.

Publish when you’re ready.

The future of survey software may not be about adding more buttons to the dashboard.

It may be about making the dashboard less necessary for the workflows you perform most often.

medium.conteudo_html: FRP products are widely used where lightweight construction, corrosion resistance and customized fabrication are important. FRP Products & Fabrication covers solutions for industrial, commercial, construction and utility applications. FRP Water Tank systems can support different water-storage requirements, while FRP Chemical Storage Tank solutions are designed for suitable chemical-handling environments. For industrial flooring, Molded FRP Gratings provide lightweight and corrosion-resistant options. FRP Roofing Sheets can be used for roofing and daylighting applications, while FRP Cooling Towers can support industrial and commercial cooling requirements.

The Build Log · 20 Sep 2026 · 2 min

AI defaults to agreeable, hedged and fast. Six prompt patterns I use to get it to disagree with me, commit to a view, and do the deep pass instead of the quick one.

Out of the box, AI assistants are agreeable. They soften bad news, hedge every claim, and give you the fast tidy answer rather than the right one. That is fine for a recipe. It is a problem when you are deciding what to build or where to put money.

These are the patterns I use every day. None of them are clever. They work because they remove the model’s permission to be vague.

1. Make it a sparring partner

Challenge this as a sparring partner. Don’t default to agreeing with me. Tell me the three strongest arguments against it before you tell me anything good.

Asking for the counter-case first stops the answer from anchoring on your framing.

2. Ask what would make it wrong

What would have to be true for this to be wrong? List the assumptions, and tell me which one is weakest.

This is the core of how my research agent writes its weekly letter: every thesis has to name its own kill conditions. If the model can’t name them, the thesis is thin.

3. Ban the hedge

Give me a high-conviction answer with specific detail. No “it depends”, no “may be worth considering”. If you’re uncertain, say how uncertain and why, once.

Hedging spread across every sentence tells you nothing. One clear statement of uncertainty tells you a lot.

4. Ask what’s wrong with the plan, not for a plan

Here is my plan. Don’t improve it. Tell me what’s missing, what I haven’t priced in, and what will break first.

When I ran a market-entry plan through this, the useful output wasn’t the plan. It was three gaps I had not thought about.

5. Push on fast answers

That came back quickly. Do a deeper pass: no stones unturned, trace it end to end, and tell me what the first pass missed.

A first review of my smart home code came back clean. The deeper pass found the entire outbound command path was dead. Full story here.

6. Scope every constraint

Constraint: no build step. Scope: the server only. The frontend can use whatever tooling it needs.

Models take constraints literally and apply them everywhere. Say what a rule covers and what it doesn’t.

All six, ready to copy: the prompt pack.

Originally published at https://cianoneill.ai.

medium.resumo: I set out to build a proper shortcuts library, not a toy. I hand-wrote the React core, then used Claude Code to take it to six frameworks…
medium.conteudo_html:
I set out to build a proper shortcuts library, not a toy. I hand-wrote the React core, then used Claude Code to take it to six frameworks in record time. Then npm nearly filibustered both of us at the finish line.

Full disclosure, right up top: I wrote the original React hook myself, by hand, no assistance. Everything past that (turning it into a proper package, generalizing it to five more frameworks, writing the test suite, and hunting down the bugs below) was done with Claude Code. I’m not burying that in a footnote. It’s the actual subject of this post.

This didn’t start as a weekend hack that accidentally grew legs. I sat down wanting to build a real shortcuts library, the kind of thing that could declare keyboard, mouse, and wheel shortcuts as plain strings, things like "CTRL+SHIFT+F", "CMD+Z", "DOUBLE_LEFT_BUTTON", and wire them up to handlers without a single hand-rolled addEventListener anywhere in your app. I built the React core myself, from scratch, no assistance. That part was always going to be React-only in my head, at first, a solid foundation before anything else.

But “something big” was the goal from day one, not an afterthought, and a shortcuts library that only works in React isn’t big, it’s a hook with a README. So rather than spend weeks personally relearning the lifecycle quirks of five frameworks I don’t use day to day, I brought in Claude Code and pointed it at the goal directly: take this React implementation and turn it into a real, multi-framework package. Quickly. What came back, and how fast it came back, is the actual subject of this post, including the part where the framework support turned out to be the easy half and the real work was a build tool arguing with itself and npm’s auth system treating us both like we were smuggling a package past customs.

TL;DR

  • The goal from day one was a real, multi-framework shortcuts library, not a side hook.
  • I wrote the React core by hand. Claude Code did the rest of what’s below, fast.
  • It pulled the event-handling logic into one framework-agnostic ShortcutsManager class.
  • Then wrote a thin adapter for each framework as its own subpath export: /react, /vue, /svelte, /solid, /preact, /angular.
  • Its own test suite caught two genuinely funny bugs in its own adapters, and fixed both.
  • Publishing got blocked by 2FA, then by a stale global npm token, then by a token scoped to the wrong account. In that order. On the same package.
  • It’s live: npm install browser-shortcuts.

01 One core, six costumes

The instinct when you want to “support more frameworks” is to go rewrite the library six times. Claude Code’s instinct, thankfully, was to resist that: six slightly-different implementations means six slightly-different bugs, forever. Instead it pulled the entire event-listening brain out of my original hook, the part that listens on window, normalizes a KeyboardEvent into a string like "CTRL+SHIFT+F", and dispatches it to listeners, into a plain class with no framework opinions at all.

class ShortcutsManager {
  on(shortcut, callback) { /* register */ }
  off(shortcut, callback) { /* unregister */ }
  attach(target = window) { /* returns a disposer */ }
}

Every framework adapter is now just this class wearing a costume appropriate to its house party: React kept my original Context Provider and useShortcut hook, rebuilt on top of the shared core. Vue got a plugin and a composable. Svelte got setupShortcuts() plus a hook that reads Svelte's context. Solid got a Provider built on its own context primitive. Angular got an injectable singleton service with DestroyRef-powered cleanup. Preact got, and I want you to sit with how funny this is, the exact same code as React, because Preact's hooks API is basically a very polite tribute act.

react preact vue svelte solid angular

One brain, six faces, and a tsup config with seven separate build entries so nobody importing browser-shortcuts/svelte accidentally drags React into their bundle.

02 The bugs were the fun part

Claude Code wrote a vitest suite that exercises the core and all six adapters: mount, fire the shortcut, unmount, confirm it stopped firing. Thirty-two tests. Along the way that suite turned up two bugs in its own freshly-written code, which it then diagnosed and fixed without me touching a line. Watching an AI catch and root-cause its own bugs is a strange kind of satisfying, like watching someone proofread their own essay out loud and actually catch the typos.

⚠ Bug 01

Solid cleaned up a cleanup function that didn’t exist

This one took the longest to run down, and it’s the kind of bug that makes you question your grip on reality. The Solid provider called onCleanup() to remove its event listeners on unmount. It compiled fine. It ran fine. It just... never actually cleaned up. No error, no warning most of the time, just a listener that outlived the component that created it.

The actual cause: in the test environment, solid-js and solid-js/web were being loaded as two separate module instances, each with its own private copy of Solid's internal "current owner" tracking variable. The component's onCleanup call registered against one copy of that variable; the root's dispose() function tore down the other. Two universes, politely ignoring each other.

Fix: since these components render no real DOM, Claude Code stopped going through solid-js/web's render() in tests entirely and drove everything through solid-js's own createRoot instead: one module, one owner, one universe.

⚠ Bug 02

Angular’s tests demanded a hazing ritual

To test one @Injectable class, it needed: zone.js (Angular's change-detection engine, which apparently just refuses to exist without it), @angular/compiler (for JIT test compilation), @angular/platform-browser-dynamic, a TestBed.initTestEnvironment() call, and a fight with Vite 8's new decorator transform before any of that would even parse. Angular decorators plus a brand-new test bundler is apparently not a combination anyone has smoothed over yet.

Fix: all of the above, added one at a time, in the order the error messages demanded them. Angular testing is basically Dark Souls with dependency injection, and I mean that as a compliment.

If your test suite doesn’t surprise you at least once, you didn’t test hard enough, and it doesn’t matter who, or what, wrote the tests.

03 Publishing: the real boss fight

Writing six framework adapters was, weirdly, the calm part of this project. The final boss was npm publish.

Round one: a flat 403, "Two-factor authentication or granular access token with bypass 2FA enabled is required to publish packages." Fine, I made a token with bypass-2FA explicitly enabled. Still failed.

Round two: turns out the token I’d carefully configured in my project’s .npmrc was being silently ignored, because the package lives inside an npm workspace and npm refuses to read a workspace member's own .npmrc for auth. The token actually being used was a stale one sitting in my global ~/.npmrc, created before I'd ever heard the words "bypass 2FA."

The actual lesson: most auth failures aren’t “is this credential valid,” they’re “which credential is even being sent.” Check that first. It’ll save you a lot of staring at error messages that are technically true but pointing at the wrong culprit.

Round three: fixed the global token, got a brand new error: a 404 on a package name that definitely exists. Turned out the new token had been scoped to the wrong account context during setup. Once that was sorted, the actual publish took about four seconds. The npm CLI does not care how much of an emotional journey you just had.

04 If you’re staring at your own single-framework library

Here’s the encouraging part, because this whole post could read like a cautionary tale and it isn’t one: generalizing a library across frameworks is genuinely more approachable than it looks from the outside, and it’s a legitimately good use of an AI pair. The pattern (one core, thin adapters) is well-established, the failure modes are well-documented across enough GitHub issues to be learnable, and the tests catch you the moment you drift. You don’t need a grand unifying abstraction. You need one honest class that does the actual work, and the discipline to keep every framework’s adapter dumb, just lifecycle glue, nothing clever. The moment an adapter starts containing real logic, you’ve built six libraries again, not one.

And write the tests, whoever’s writing the code. Not because tests are virtuous, but because they’re the fastest way to find out where the mental model of “how this framework works” is quietly wrong. Both bugs above were a gap between what was assumed and what was actually true, and they only surfaced because a test insisted on checking.

I’ll say the quiet part plainly, since it’s the actual point of this post: I wrote the React hook, Claude Code wrote the rest of what’s above, and I’m comfortable putting my name on both halves. It’s live now, MIT-licensed, zero runtime dependencies of its own:

npm install browser-shortcuts
  • browser-shortcuts/react and /preact: a Provider and a useShortcut hook
  • browser-shortcuts/vue: a plugin and a composable
  • browser-shortcuts/svelte: setupShortcuts() plus a hook
  • browser-shortcuts/solid: a context Provider
  • browser-shortcuts/angular: an injectable service

If you use one of these frameworks and shortcuts in your app currently involve a stray addEventListener in a useEffect somewhere, I'd love for you to try it and tell me what breaks. That's genuinely the fastest way to find bug number three.

Side note

This isn’t the first thing I’ve shipped to npm, and it won’t be the last. If you’re curious what else is out there:

  • antoniookoro.com, my portfolio, with writing, projects, and how to reach me
  • vue3-form, form validation for Vue 3 and the composition API
  • bootstrap-vue-datatable, a datatable plugin for Vue and Bootstrap
  • storagedotjs, a small, lightweight API over Local Storage

Written by Antonio Okoro, built with Claude Code.
Thoughts, bug reports, and “well actually”s about Solid’s owner tracking are all welcome.

medium.titulo: Building Accessible Vue Components: A Developer-First Approach
medium.resumo: Practical patterns for making accessibility part of component development before issues reach QA or production.
medium.conteudo_html:
Practical patterns for making accessibility part of component development before issues reach QA or production.

In my previous article, Shifting Accessibility Left: Bringing Accessibility Into the Developer Workflow, I discussed a simple idea: accessibility feedback becomes much more useful when it reaches developers while software is being built.

But what does that actually look like in code?

For front-end developers, one of the most effective places to start is the component layer.

Modern applications are built from reusable pieces. Buttons, inputs, modals, dropdowns, cards, navigation elements, and entire interaction patterns are implemented once and reused throughout an application.

That creates an interesting consequence.

When an accessibility problem exists inside a reusable component, the problem scales. When accessibility is built into that component correctly, the solution scales too.

That is why accessible component development should be treated as an engineering concern rather than something we only look at during QA.

Let’s look at what that means in practice using Vue.

A component can work perfectly and still be inaccessible

Consider something as simple as a clickable element:

<template>
  <div
    class="button"
    @click="addToCart"
  >
    Add to Cart
  </div>
</template>

From a visual perspective, this can easily look like a button.

We can style it. We can attach a click handler. We can make it behave correctly with a mouse.

From a basic functional testing perspective, someone might conclude:

It works.

But that conclusion depends heavily on how the person interacts with the application.

A <div> does not automatically have button semantics. It is not keyboard-operable like a native button, and assistive technologies do not receive the same information they would receive from an actual <button>.

The simplest improvement is also the most important one:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="button"
    @click="addToCart"
  >
    Add to Cart
  </button>
</template>

This small change gives us a surprising amount of behavior for free.

The browser already understands what a button is. Keyboard interaction works as expected. Assistive technologies can identify the element correctly, and focus behavior follows established browser conventions.

This illustrates one of the most useful accessibility principles in front-end development:

Use native HTML semantics whenever they already describe the interaction you are building.

ARIA is extremely valuable, but it should not be used to recreate behavior that HTML already provides.

Accessibility starts at the component API

The problem becomes more interesting when we turn that button into a reusable component.

Imagine a generic icon button:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="icon-button"
    @click="$emit('click')"
  >
    <Icon :name="icon" />
  </button>
</template>

Visually, the icon may communicate the action perfectly.

A trash icon means delete. A magnifying glass means search. An X means close.

But visual meaning is not necessarily an accessible name.

We can expose that requirement through the component API:

<template>
  <button
    type="button"
    class="icon-button"
    :aria-label="label"
    @click="$emit('click')"
  >
    <Icon
      :name="icon"
      aria-hidden="true"
    />
  </button>
</template>
<script>
export default {
  props: {
    icon: {
      type: String,
      required: true
    },
    label: {
      type: String,
      required: true
    }
  }
}
</script>

Now the developer consuming the component has to provide the information it needs:

<IconButton
  icon="trash"
  label="Delete item"
/>

This changes something important in the architecture.

Instead of hoping every developer remembers to add accessibility later, we design the component so that using it correctly naturally encourages accessible behavior.

Accessibility becomes part of the component’s API contract.

Reusable components multiply decisions

Suppose an application uses the same button component in 100 different places.

If that component has poor keyboard behavior, we potentially created the same accessibility problem 100 times.

If we try to fix each implementation individually, we now have 100 places to verify and maintain.

But if the behavior belongs inside a shared component, a single improvement can propagate throughout the application.

The same principle applies to form controls, navigation, dropdowns, accordions, dialogs, tabs, notifications, tooltips, and interactive cards.

This is one reason design systems and component libraries can play such an important role in accessibility.

They are not just tools for visual consistency.

They are also distribution mechanisms for engineering decisions.

Accessibility is one of those decisions.

Keyboard support should not be an afterthought

Mouse interaction is usually the easiest path to test during development.

Click something.

It works.

Move on.

But a useful habit is to occasionally put the mouse aside and navigate the interface using only the keyboard.

There are a few simple questions worth asking:

Can I reach the interactive element with Tab?

Can I tell where the focus currently is?

Can I activate the control using the expected keyboard interaction?

Can I leave the component without getting trapped?

Does focus move somewhere unexpected after an action?

These checks become especially important when we build custom interactive components.

Consider a clickable product card:

<template>
  <div @click="openProduct(product)">
    <h3>{{ product.name }}</h3>
    <p>{{ product.description }}</p>
  </div>
</template>

It can be tempting to add tabindex, keyboard listeners, roles, and additional ARIA attributes until the <div> behaves like an interactive control.

Sometimes a custom interaction genuinely requires additional behavior.

But before doing that, there is a better engineering question to ask:

Is there already a native HTML element that represents this interaction?

If clicking the card performs navigation, perhaps the component should contain an <a>.

If it performs an action, perhaps it should use a <button>.

Choosing the correct semantic foundation can eliminate entire categories of accessibility bugs before they exist.

ARIA should add meaning, not compensate for architecture

ARIA is sometimes treated as the accessibility layer of an application.

That can lead to implementations like this:

<div
  role="button"
  tabindex="0"
  aria-label="Add to Cart"
>
  Add to Cart
</div>

The markup now communicates more information to assistive technology, but we have also taken responsibility for reproducing behavior that a native button already provides.

We may need to handle keyboard activation ourselves.

We need to maintain focus behavior.

We need to make sure different states are communicated correctly.

We also need to test those behaviors across browsers and assistive technologies.

Compare that with:

<button type="button">
  Add to Cart
</button>

The second implementation is not simply shorter.

It transfers responsibility for established interaction behavior back to the browser.

In most cases, that’s exactly what we want.

Start with semantic HTML. Use ARIA when additional semantics or state are actually necessary.

Accessible states matter too

Accessibility is not limited to the initial state of a component.

Modern interfaces constantly change.

Buttons become disabled. Forms display errors. Content loads asynchronously. Menus expand and collapse. Dialogs appear. Notifications are generated.

A component therefore needs to communicate not only what it is, but sometimes what is happening to it.

Consider a loading button:

<template>
  <button
    type="submit"
    :disabled="loading"
  >
    {{ loading ? 'Processing...' : 'Place Order' }}
  </button>
</template>

Changing the visible text is already useful.

Depending on the interaction, additional techniques may be appropriate for communicating asynchronous changes to assistive technologies.

But the larger engineering principle is more important:

Accessibility needs to follow component state.

If the UI changes visually but that change is not represented semantically, different users may effectively be interacting with different versions of the application.

Focus is part of application state

Dialogs are a good example.

Opening a modal is visually obvious.

For keyboard and screen reader users, however, focus management becomes part of the interaction.

When a dialog opens, we need to think about a few things.

Where should focus go?

Can the user navigate outside the dialog?

What happens when the dialog closes?

Should focus return to the element that opened it?

These aren’t just visual design details. They are part of the component’s behavior.

Once again, implementing this correctly inside a shared dialog component is much safer than asking every feature or developer to solve the same problem independently.

A well-designed component can encapsulate styles, markup, functionality, and accessible interaction behavior.

Accessibility belongs in the definition of a component

We often define component quality using characteristics such as reusable, responsive, performant, maintainable, and testable.

I believe accessible belongs on that list too.

A component that works only for a subset of interaction methods is not fully implemented.

This doesn’t mean every front-end developer needs to become an accessibility specialist.

It means accessibility should influence the same engineering decisions we already make every day.

Which HTML element should I use?

What should this component expose through props?

What states need to be represented?

How should keyboard interaction work?

Where should focus move?

Can this behavior be solved once inside the shared component instead of repeatedly across the application?

These are engineering questions.

And treating them that way changes when accessibility enters the development process.

Automated tools help, but they don’t understand everything

Linting, browser audits, automated accessibility testing, and CI checks can catch many common problems.

They can identify missing accessible names, invalid ARIA attributes, certain contrast issues, and some semantic problems.

These tools are valuable because they provide fast feedback.

But accessibility cannot be reduced to a score.

An automated tool cannot fully determine whether an interaction makes sense. It cannot always understand whether focus moves somewhere logical. It cannot guarantee that a complex workflow is understandable with a screen reader.

And most importantly, passing an automated accessibility test does not automatically mean the experience is usable.

Automation should support human judgment, not replace it.

What if this feedback appeared while we were coding?

This brings me back to the idea from my previous article.

Imagine writing a Vue component and receiving feedback directly inside the development environment:

AccessibleButton.vue

✓ Native button semantics
✓ Keyboard accessible
✓ Accessible name available
⚠ Focus state may not be visible
✓ No conflicting ARIA attributes

Instead of discovering these issues days or weeks later during QA, developers could address many of them while the component is still fresh in their minds.

Even more interestingly, tooling could understand component patterns rather than looking only at the final HTML.

It could analyze templates.

Props.

Interactive handlers.

ARIA usage.

Potential keyboard interactions.

Reusable component APIs.

That would move accessibility feedback closer to the moment when engineering decisions are actually being made.

And I think developer tooling still has a lot of room to explore here.

Build accessibility once, distribute it everywhere

Component-driven development gives us leverage.

That leverage works in both directions.

A poorly designed component can distribute accessibility problems across an entire product.

A thoughtfully designed component can distribute good accessibility practices just as efficiently.

Shifting accessibility left doesn’t necessarily mean adding another complicated stage to the development process.

Sometimes it starts with something much simpler.

Choosing a <button> instead of a <div>.

Making accessible names part of a component API.

Testing keyboard behavior before opening a pull request.

Managing focus inside shared interaction patterns.

Building accessibility into the components that other developers will reuse.

The earlier these decisions happen, the less accessibility feels like remediation.

It simply becomes part of building the component correctly.

That leaves me with another question I want to explore:

What if our development tools could help us make these decisions before the component ever leaves the editor?

That’s where I’d like to go next.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: MARATONA DE BUENOS AIRES supera o Rio e é a MAIOR da América do Sul
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Buenos Aires supera o Rio e volta a ser a maior maratona da América do Sul. Entenda por que atletas foram desclassificados por chegarem de mãos dadas e confira os resultados dos brasileiros no Mundial de Corrida de Rua e na ASICS Run Challenge de Recife.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Segunda-feira | 21 de setembro de 2026

A Maratona de Buenos Aires voltou a ser a maior prova de 42 km da América do Sul. A edição de 2026 registrou um crescimento de 13% no número de concluintes em relação a 2025, ultrapassando a Maratona do Rio por uma margem de apenas 34 corredores. Foram 14.209 finishers na capital argentina, contra 14.175 na cidade brasileira, que havia sido a maior no ano anterior.

No masculino, a vitória foi do queniano Betwel Kibet Chumba, com 2h08m28s. O pódio foi completado por John Hakizimana, de Ruanda (2h08m39s), e os quenianos Felix Kiptoo Kirwa (2h10m24s), Kipkemoi Kiprono (2h10m49s) e Vincent Kiber Raimoi (2h11m58s). Entre as mulheres, a queniana Rebecca Kangogo Chesir venceu com 2h23m36s, seguida por sua compatriota Rodah Jepkorir Tanui (2h24m49s) e a também queniana Emnah Cheruto Ndiiwa (2h26m55s). As etíopes Sintayehu Lewetegn Hailemichael e Ageru Arera Tamir fecharam o pódio feminino.

Atletas são desclassificados por chegarem de mãos dadas

Na Corrida da Saúde Farmácia Brito, em Feira de Santana (BA), os atletas Justino Pedro e Givaldo Sena foram desclassificados após cruzarem a linha de chegada de mãos dadas. Ambos são da mesma equipe e, ao abrirem mão da disputa pela vitória, infringiram a regra da World Athletics sobre “esforço autêntico” (“bona fide effort”).

A regra 7.1 do regulamento de atletismo estabelece que atletas devem participar de competições com “esforço autêntico” e que qualquer um que não cumpra essa diretriz pode ser desclassificado. Ao não disputarem a primeira colocação entre si, os corredores deixaram de competir, o que caracteriza a falta de esforço autêntico e justifica a decisão do árbitro da prova. O treinador dos atletas, Marciano Barros, contestou o resultado e pediu que a decisão fosse reconsiderada. No entanto, a regra é clara e tem sido aplicada com mais rigor nos últimos anos para garantir a integridade da competição.

Minha experiência na ASICS Run Challenge do Recife

Participei da etapa do Recife da ASICS Run Challenge, correndo os 15 km. A prova foi excelente, com um percurso lindo que passou por pontos icônicos da cidade, como o Forte do Brum, diversas pontes, o Marco Zero e o Leão do Norte. A largada, às 5h30 da manhã, ajudou a amenizar o calor, que ficou na média de 24°C. O vento e a brisa também contribuíram para diminuir a sensação térmica.

A hidratação foi um ponto positivo, com água gelada em todos os postos, a cada 3 km. O único aspecto negativo foi um atraso de quase 10 minutos na largada. Completei a prova em 1h28m28s. Uma observação sobre a medalha é que ela não traz a identificação da cidade, sendo idêntica à de outras etapas do circuito.

Brasileiros competem no Mundial de Corrida de Rua

O Mundial de Corrida de Rua, realizado em Copenhague, contou com a participação de atletas brasileiros em diversas distâncias. Confira os principais resultados:
